Scope warning: This case series documents a clinical signal in three patients. It does not estimate incidence, establish COVID-19 as the cause of pneumomediastinum, compare management strategies, or validate a screening protocol. The reported drug regimens are exposure history, not evidence of efficacy.

One-page synthesis

Core thesis: Pneumomediastinum can occur during severe COVID-19 pneumonia even without antecedent positive-pressure ventilation or known pre-existing pulmonary disease, and delayed onset may accompany new chest pain or worsening hypoxemia.

The report presents three hospitalized Hispanic men (ages 51, 37, and 34 years), all non-smokers, with severe SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia/ARDS and reported PaO2:FiO2 ratios of 68, 80, and 59. Pneumomediastinum was recognized on hospital days 15, 14, and 36, respectively. Case 1 also had a small right apical pneumothorax requiring chest-tube placement; Case 2 had a small amount of pneumopericardium; Case 3's pneumomediastinum was attributed by the authors as likely related to violent coughing.

All three cases ultimately improved enough for discharge while still requiring supplemental oxygen. The article's practical message is diagnostic vigilance: consider pneumomediastinum when severe COVID-19 patients develop new chest pain or worsening dyspnea/hypoxemia and use repeat chest radiography to recognize it. That message is plausible and directly grounded in the cases, but the design cannot determine frequency, risk factors, mechanism, or whether conservative management is superior to alternatives.

Section condensation

Abstract

The abstract frames pneumomediastinum as an uncommon but clinically important manifestation of COVID-19 and summarizes three affected Hispanic men. It highlights absence of smoking history and positive-pressure ventilation, argues that frequent chest radiography can support early recognition, and warns that an otherwise usually benign process can produce morbidity if missed.

Introduction

The introduction positions the report within early-2020 knowledge: pneumothorax had been described as uncommon/rare and spontaneous pneumomediastinum had only a small number of case reports. The authors define the distinguishing features of their series as three non-smokers without underlying pulmonary disease or positive-pressure ventilation, with pneumomediastinum developing two weeks or more after admission.

Cases

Case 1: A 51-year-old obese Hispanic man with severe ARDS (P/F 68) developed sudden chest pain and worsening hypoxemia on day 15; radiography showed pneumomediastinum and a small right apical pneumothorax. A chest tube improved oxygenation, the air leaks resolved, and he was discharged to rehabilitation on 3 L/min oxygen. At 8 weeks, CT showed peripheral ground-glass opacities with bronchiectasis but no significant bullous disease.

Case 2: A 37-year-old obese Hispanic man with severe ARDS (P/F 80) developed pneumomediastinum on day 14 while needing 15 L/min NRB plus 6 L/min nasal cannula. CT showed extensive bilateral ground-glass opacification, diffuse pneumomediastinum, and a small pneumopericardium without significant bullous disease. He was managed conservatively and discharged after 27 days on 2 L/min oxygen; follow-up radiography still showed pneumomediastinum but improved consolidations.

Case 3: A 34-year-old Hispanic man with severe ARDS (P/F 59) had no pulmonary embolism or bullous disease on CT. Hypoxemia worsened; he refused intubation on day 18. Pneumomediastinum appeared on day 36 and was described as likely secondary to violent coughing. Conservative management was followed by radiographic resolution before discharge after six weeks on 2 L/min oxygen.

Discussion

The authors invoke the classic alveolar-rupture/perivascular-air-tracking mechanism and argue that pneumomediastinum should remain in the differential diagnosis when severe SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia is accompanied by new chest pain or worsening shortness of breath. They note possible complications such as tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, subcutaneous emphysema, and pneumorrhachis, and recommend repeat chest radiography for recognition.

They state that conservative management is usually preferred but acknowledge possible cardiorespiratory compromise. Importantly, they also state that the exact mechanism of pneumomediastinum in COVID-19 remains unclear and call for further research.

Competing interests

The authors report none.

Evaluation and appraisal

Verdict: Skim deeply. Best used as an early signal-description paper and for recognizing a plausible non-ventilator-associated air-leak phenotype. Do not use it to estimate incidence, assign causality, choose COVID-19 pharmacotherapy, or compare pneumomediastinum management strategies.
6/10
Relevance

Clinically relevant as an early signal of spontaneous pneumomediastinum in severe COVID-19 without positive-pressure ventilation.

Evidence basis: Three directly described cases with imaging-confirmed events.

Limiting factor: Narrow disease-era and phenotype scope.

Would change score: Higher if linked to contemporary incidence/outcome cohorts or current management questions.

7/10
Novelty

At publication, the report added an early three-case series focused on non-ventilated patients.

Evidence basis: Authors identified only a small number of prior case reports and contrasted with ventilated cases.

Limiting factor: Novelty is time-dependent and does not imply strong evidence.

Would change score: Lower when later, larger cohorts reproduce the phenotype; higher only if unique mechanistic data existed.

2/10
Method strength

An uncontrolled, three-patient descriptive case series is appropriate for signal description but weak for causal or comparative inference.

Evidence basis: Individual timelines and imaging are reported.

Limiting factor: No comparator, sampling frame, incidence denominator, prespecified methods, or statistical analysis.

Would change score: A prospective cohort with explicit case ascertainment and comparator groups would raise the score.

3/10
Evidence strength

The source supports that pneumomediastinum can occur in these three non-ventilated COVID-19 patients, but not how often, why, or whether management changes outcomes.

Evidence basis: Direct case-level clinical and radiographic observations.

Limiting factor: Small n, no control group, no causal design, no uncertainty estimates.

Would change score: Larger multicenter cohorts with adjusted analyses and validated event ascertainment would raise the score.

2/10
External validity

Generalizability is very limited by the single-center, three-patient sample and uniform demographic profile.

Evidence basis: All patients were hospitalized Hispanic men with severe ARDS.

Limiting factor: No women, mild disease, other settings, or comparative population.

Would change score: Broader multicenter sampling across disease severity and demographics would raise the score.

4/10
Implementation value

Useful mainly for diagnostic vigilance and recognition of an air-leak phenotype, not for treatment selection.

Evidence basis: Timelines link new chest pain/hypoxemia to chest imaging; all cases were managed without prior positive-pressure ventilation.

Limiting factor: No comparative diagnostic strategy or management-effectiveness evidence.

Would change score: Prospective evidence on screening triggers and management outcomes would raise the score.

Main strengths

  • Direct case-level clinical timelines and radiographic documentation.
  • Consistent focus on absence of positive-pressure ventilation and reported underlying bullous disease.
  • All three main-text figures are linked to the individual cases.

Main limitations

  • Only three patients from one institution and no comparator or denominator.
  • No formal Methods section, explicit case-ascertainment strategy, or statistical analysis.
  • Cannot distinguish disease-related alveolar injury from coughing, oxygen support, unmeasured lung vulnerability, or other contributors.
  • Management conclusions are not comparative; clinical improvement after conservative care does not establish treatment effectiveness.

Confidence in appraisal: High for judging the evidentiary limits of this design; moderate for broader clinical relevance because that depends on later evidence not evaluated in this source-only appraisal.

Implementation / practice takeaways

Use

Recognize pneumomediastinum as a possible complication in severe COVID-19 even before intubation/positive-pressure ventilation.

Monitor

New chest pain, worsening dyspnea, or unexplained hypoxemia were the clinical changes highlighted by the authors as reasons to repeat chest imaging.

Do not overclaim

The series does not establish screening frequency, incidence, causal mechanism, or superiority of conservative treatment.
